title: Wood Mackenzie projects EU inverter restrictions could cut forecast solar and storage installations at least 5% in Central and Eastern Europe through 2030
gist: Wood Mackenzie (in a SolarPower Europe-commissioned study) estimates the European Commission's April 2026 restriction on 'high-risk' (incl. all Chinese) inverters in EU-financed projects exposes 21+ GW of PV and 13 GW of storage inverter demand in 2027-2030, cutting Central and Eastern European solar/storage forecasts ~5-6% in the base case and up to 18% under a full Cyber Security Act ban. Western capacity (>150 GW by end-2027) is adequate on paper, but local sales/after-sales infrastructure, lead times and razor-thin project margins drive demand attrition.

insights.claim: In April 2026 the European Commission barred 'high-risk' inverters from all solar and storage projects receiving EU institution loans or direct EU funding, and with the 1 November 2026 grandfathering deadline passed, over 21 GW of European PV inverter demand is exposed between 2027 and 2030.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Policy is now binding on EU-financed pipelines; utility-scale solar and storage carry most of the exposed capacity.
insights.locator: In April 2026, the European Commission restricted

insights.claim: All China-headquartered inverter manufacturers fall under the EU 'high-risk' designation, and Chinese suppliers held over 80% of inverter shipments to Europe in 2025, with even higher shares in price-sensitive markets most reliant on EU funding.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: An 80%+ incumbent share being policy-excluded is a large market-share transfer opportunity for non-Chinese inverter vendors.
insights.locator: Notably, all inverter manufacturers headquartered in China

insights.claim: The EU funding-based inverter restrictions are expected to be followed by broader critical-grid-infrastructure protections, including revisions to the Cyber Security Act that could amount to a full ban on 'high-risk' inverters.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The current rule is likely a first step; the bigger risk/opportunity is a private-sector-wide ban via the Cyber Security Act.
insights.locator: The European Commission's decision came as a response

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie notes the European Commission had not officially published a statement or document detailing the April 2026 inverter decision, so the restrictions' scope is understood only from public statements, press releases and stakeholder conversations.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Regulatory ambiguity itself is a cost: expect contract renegotiations and conservative procurement until scope is formalised.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie estimates non-high-risk inverter manufacturing capacity available to Europe will exceed 150 GW by end-2027, enough on paper to meet the region's solar and storage inverter demand.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Aggregate capacity is not the bottleneck — the constraint is localized go-to-market, which favours vendors with existing CEE footprints.
insights.locator: Western inverter vendors will need to play a significant role

insights.claim: Central and Eastern European stakeholders report it could take months or years for western inverter vendors to build adequate local sales and after-sales infrastructure, even where already certified, and longer lead times on large orders could delay utility-scale projects.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Vendors investing in CEE service networks now can capture share; developers face near-term schedule risk on big EU-funded projects.
insights.locator: Stakeholders in CEE reported a disconnect

insights.claim: CEE is more exposed than the rest of the EU to inverter restrictions because more of its projects rely on EU loans and funding and because Chinese vendors dominate those price-sensitive markets with established sales and after-sales networks.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: CEE solar/storage developers and installers are the most vulnerable segment; Western Europe is comparatively insulated.
insights.locator: The Central and Eastern Europe region faces significantly higher exposure

insights.claim: Swapping away from Chinese inverters can raise system-level PV and storage project prices by 2-10% even though inverters are a small share of total costs, and some developers say cost increases as low as 1-5% could break already razor-thin margins.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Price sensitivity, not supply, is the main driver of installation losses — margin-thin developers in EU-funded markets are at risk.
insights.locator: Even as western vendors make necessary business expansions

insights.claim: Europe's most popular energy storage products are AC-blocks integrating battery and inverter from a single vendor, so decoupling Chinese integrated solutions will raise average prices and complicate installation and warranty processes.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The restriction reaches into battery storage system integration, not just standalone inverters — a tailwind for non-Chinese integrated BESS suppliers.
insights.locator: Market challenges extend beyond direct inverter procurement

insights.claim: EPCs and installers in Central and Eastern Europe expect an added cost burden from training staff to work with unfamiliar non-Chinese inverter models.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Transition costs extend down to the installer layer, adding friction beyond hardware price premiums.
insights.locator: Additionally, EPCs and installers in CEE

insights.claim: About 14% of European PV projects and 10% of storage projects rely on EU-backed loans and funding, exposing over 21 GW of PV and 13 GW of storage inverter demand to the 'high-risk' restrictions in 2027-2030.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Sizes the directly affected pipeline — a minority of European projects but concentrated in specific markets.

insights.claim: In Wood Mackenzie's base case, 2027-2030 PV installations across major CEE markets decline an average 6% and storage 5% versus pre-restriction conditions, with Romania, Czechia and Bulgaria most impacted; Europe-wide the four-year solar and storage forecast falls only 3%, concentrated in 2027.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Downgrade exposure to Romanian, Czech and Bulgarian solar/storage volumes, especially 2027; Western European markets largely unaffected.
insights.locator: Across major CEE markets, Wood Mackenzie estimates

insights.claim: Under a high-severity scenario modelling a full EU-wide ban on 'high-risk' inverters enforced by 2029, four-year CEE installation losses exceed 18% for solar and 13% for storage, and EU-wide declines reach 11% for solar and 13% for storage, concentrated in 2029-2030.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The Cyber Security Act revision is the tail risk to European solar/storage volumes and a major upside for non-Chinese inverter makers.
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie also considered a high-severity impact scenario

insights.claim: The Wood Mackenzie inverter-restriction study was commissioned by SolarPower Europe, an industry body, though Wood Mackenzie says its findings are independent and it makes no policy recommendations.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Weigh the study's demand-attrition estimates with the commissioning industry association's interest in mind.
insights.locator: This publicly available report was commissioned by SolarPower Europe
